newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says no EU meat deal, but odds have improved.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says no EU meat deal, but odds have improved.

text.p: Senior U.S. Agriculture Department trade official Paul Drazek said Thursday that 2-1/2 days of talks with the European Union to settle a dispute over meat imports had not yielded an agreement, but the "odds have improved."
"We have made some progress since April 1...therefore, it would be safe to say that the odds have improved" toward reaching an agreement," Drazek said in a press briefing.
U.S. and EU officials have been meeting this week to reach a deal in the veterinary equivalency talks that affect hundreds of millions of dollars of trans-Altantic trade.

Asked if Washington would extend its April 15 deadline to delist over 100 EU meat and poultry packing plants if they cannot comply with U.S. standards, Drazek said, "I don't think there's a possibility of that."

Drazek said that many difficult issues had been settled, including an agreement that would allow $30 million worth of U.S. dairy products to continue to be shipped to the EU, the most contentious points remained.

Decontamination in U.S. poultry processing appears to be the key sticking point. The U.S. industry uses chlorine in anti-bacterial rinses. The EU has said it would only consider the use of lactic acid or TSP in decontamination.
The European Union has offered to do a scientific review of U.S. hygenic practices in meat and poultry processing sectors, and to specifically target the use of decontamination in poultry plants.
But the plan would only study the use of lactic acid and TSP in the decontamination process, and not of chlorine.
Drazek said that was a concern to U.S. negotiators.

Asked if the exclusion of chlorine could end up to be a deal-breaker, Drazek said he did not want to comment on what was and was not a deal-breaker, but said, "It's an important question -- no doubt about it."
Drazek said the U.S. objective is "to have chlorine accepted -- period."
He said chlorination is a perfectly safe method and that the use of decontaminants results in a "much, much safer product."

The USDA official said the two sides will remain in contact Friday in an attempt to reach an agreement. EU officials had originally planned to leave Washington Thursday but announced earlier that they were staying for further talks.
